passages.title: Received gifts require growth while remembered witness supports the coming promise
passages.summary: Simon Peter writes to those who share the same precious faith. God’s power has given them all they need for life and godliness. Through his promises they share in the divine nature. They are to add goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, affection, and love to faith. With these they will not be idle or unfruitful. Peter says he will soon put off his tent and wants them to remember. He was an eyewitness of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain. Prophecy came as the Holy Spirit moved men, not by human will.
passages.uncertainty: No exact location is assigned to unnamed or heavenly settings.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects growing Christlike qualities with developing our divine nature. How does growth in love prevent received knowledge from remaining idle?

contextNote.title: Received gifts require growth while remembered witness supports the coming promise
contextNote.text: Verses 3–4 say God has given everything needed and great promises. Verses 5–7 list what to add, from faith through to love. Verse 8 gives the result if these qualities are theirs and growing. They will not be idle or unfruitful in knowing the Lord Jesus Christ. Knowledge is meant to bear fruit. Verse 9 says one who lacks them is blind and forgets his cleansing. Verse 10 tells them to make their calling sure.

passages.title: Promises of freedom conceal greed and renewed slavery when conduct denies the message
passages.summary: Peter warns that false teachers will come among them, as false prophets did. In greed they will exploit the readers with made-up words. God did not spare the angels who sinned or the ancient world. He saved Noah and rescued Lot from Sodom. These teachers despise authority and are like unreasoning animals. They have followed the way of Balaam, who loved the wages of wrongdoing. They are springs without water. They promise freedom, and their last state is worse than the first.
passages.uncertainty: No exact location is assigned to unnamed or heavenly settings.

lds.text: Why can promised freedom become a form of slavery when conduct remains corrupt?

contextNote.title: Promises of freedom conceal greed and renewed slavery when conduct denies the message
contextNote.text: Verse 18 says these teachers entice people who are just escaping from error. Verse 19 names the bait: a promise of liberty. It then names the teachers’ real condition: they are bondservants of corruption. The verse gives a general rule to prove it. A person is a slave of whatever overcomes him. Verses 20–22 apply it to those who return to the world’s defilements. Their last state is worse than the first.

passages.title: The delayed promise calls for patient hope and changed conduct without an exact countdown
passages.summary: Peter says this is his second letter and reminds them of the prophets’ words. Mockers will ask where the promise of his coming is. They forget that the world was once destroyed by water. The present heavens and earth are kept for fire. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years. The day of the Lord will come like a thief. They should live in holiness and look for new heavens and a new earth. Peter mentions Paul’s letters, which some twist.
passages.uncertainty: No exact location is assigned to unnamed or heavenly settings.

lds.text: How does patient waiting change present conduct without supplying a date for the coming day?

contextNote.title: The delayed promise calls for patient hope and changed conduct without an exact countdown
contextNote.text: Verse 4 gives the mockers’ argument: nothing has changed since the fathers died. Verse 8 answers about time: a thousand years are as a day. Verse 9 answers about motive. The delay is not slowness; it is patience. God does not wish anyone to perish. He wants all to come to repentance. Verse 15 repeats it: count the Lord’s patience as salvation.
